units.title: The five vowels
units.can: pronounce あ い う え お cleanly and hear them in real words.
units.pattern: あ ・ い ・ う ・ え ・ お
units.explain: Japanese has five short vowels, and they do not slide into each other the way English vowels do. Keep the mouth still for each one. あ is open, い is spread, う is loose and unrounded, え is in between, お is round but not deep. Say them five times slowly, then use them in words.
units.form: Five vowels, five moras: あ い う え お. Each one is short and pure.
units.pitfall: English speakers glide あ into え, or お into う. Keep the mouth still for the whole mora.

units.title: Beat, long vowel, small っ
units.can: hear the difference between a short sound, a held sound and a one-beat silence.
units.pattern: おばさん → おばあさん ・ きて → きって
units.explain: Japanese is timed in beats called mora. A long vowel is two beats; the small っ is one beat of silence. These are not decoration: they change the word. おばさん is aunt, おばあさん is grandmother. きて is “come”, きって is a postage stamp.
units.form: Long vowel: hold the vowel for two moras (おばあさん). Small っ: one mora of silence before the next sound (きって).
units.pitfall: A small っ is not a pause for breath, it is a beat. きて and きって differ in length, not in emphasis.

units.title: Hiragana: ka and sa rows
units.can: read and write か き く け こ and さ し す せ そ.
units.pattern: か き く け こ ／ さ し す せ そ
units.explain: Hiragana is the native syllabary: one shape, one sound. Learn it in rows of five. Write each character large, then small, saying the sound out loud each time. し is “shi”, not “si”; す is a light “su”, not “soo”.
units.form: か row: か き く け こ. さ row: さ し す せ そ. し is “shi”, never “si”.
units.pitfall: す is made with unrounded lips. Do not round it into the “su” of English “soon”.

units.title: Hiragana: ta and na rows
units.can: read た ち つ て と and な に ぬ ね の inside short words.
units.pattern: た ち つ て と ／ な に ぬ ね の
units.explain: Two sounds need extra care: ち is “chi”, and つ is “tsu”, made by briefly touching the tongue behind the top teeth. ぬ and ね differ only by the final loop; slow writing fixes them faster than fast writing.
units.form: た row: た ち つ て と. な row: な に ぬ ね の. ち is “chi”, つ is “tsu”.
units.pitfall: つ is not “tu”. Put the tongue behind the top teeth and release a little air.

units.title: Hiragana: the rest of the chart
units.can: read the は, ま, や, ら and わ rows, plus ん.
units.pattern: は ひ ふ へ ほ ／ ま み む め も ／ や ゆ よ ／ ら り る れ ろ ／ わ を ん
units.explain: The last rows complete the chart. ふ is not “fu” with English teeth on lips; it is a soft puff between the lips. を is used only as a particle, and ん is a full beat of its own. At this point you can read any hiragana word, even if you do not know it yet.
units.form: は row, ま row, や row (や ゆ よ), ら row, then わ を ん. The particle を is pronounced “o”.
units.pitfall: ら り る れ ろ is a single tongue tap, close to the “tt” in American “butter”, not an English “r”.

units.title: Voiced sounds and small や
units.can: read が ざ だ ば ぱ and combinations such as きゃ しゅ ちょ.
units.pattern: が ぎ ぐ げ ご ・ きゃ きゅ きょ
units.explain: Two small marks (゛) voice a consonant: か → が, さ → ざ, た → だ, は → ば. A small circle (゜) makes the p row: は → ぱ. A small や, ゆ or よ glides the previous sound into one beat: きゃ is “kya”, not “ki-ya”.
units.form: Voiced marks give が ざ だ ば; the semi-voiced mark gives ぱ. A small や/ゆ/よ after an i-row kana makes one mora: きゃ きゅ きょ.
units.pitfall: きゃ is one beat; きや is two. Do not slip a vowel between the consonants.

units.title: Katakana and loanwords
units.can: recognise the katakana shapes for coffee, bread, hotel and taxi.
units.pattern: コーヒー ・ パン ・ ホテル ・ タクシー
units.explain: Katakana is the same 46 sounds in angular shapes. It marks loanwords, foreign names, sound effects and emphasis. The long vowel mark ー holds the previous vowel for one more beat: コーヒー is ko-o-hi-i, four beats.
units.form: Katakana writes loanwords. Long vowels use ー: コーヒー, タクシー.
units.pitfall: Katakana is not a code for English spelling. パン is “pan” meaning bread, not a frying pan.

units.title: Greetings for the time of day
units.can: greet someone in the morning, afternoon and evening, and thank them.
units.pattern: おはようございます ・ こんにちは ・ こんばんは ・ ありがとうございます
units.explain: Greetings are the first place where standard and Kansai part company. Use the standard polite forms with people you do not know. The Kansai examples have different social settings: まいど is associated with shops and familiar customers, not a general replacement for こんにちは. おおきに is a regional way to thank someone; many Osaka speakers also use ありがとう.
units.form: おはようございます (morning), こんにちは (day), こんばんは (evening), ありがとうございます (thanks).
units.pitfall: こんにちは ends in は, not わ. It is a fixed greeting, not the topic particle.

units.title: Polite verbs: ます and ません
units.can: say what you do, do not do, and ask a polite question.

units.can: mark the thing that receives an action.

units.explain: へ (pronounced “e”) points the direction. で marks where an action happens. に marks a destination, a time, or the person you meet. They overlap at the edges, so learn them in whole phrases rather than as one-to-one translations.

units.title: The て-form: joining actions
units.can: link two actions in one sentence and make a casual request.
units.pattern: たべて → たべて、ねる ・ ちょっと まって
units.explain: The て-form is the connector of Japanese. It joins actions (たべて、ねます = eat and sleep), makes requests (まって = wait), and forms the progressive (たべています). Learn it as a shape, not a translation: う/つ/る → って, む/ぶ/ぬ → んで, く → いて, す → して.
units.form: V-て + V. The final verb carries the tense and the politeness.
units.pitfall: Only the last verb needs ます. たべて、のみます is fine; two ます forms sound like two separate sentences.

units.can: say what you can and cannot do, and ask about ability.
units.pattern: たべられます ・ いけます ・ できます
units.explain: Polite potential verbs end in 〜えます or 〜られます: たべる → たべられます, いく → いけます, する → できます. The object often takes が: にほんごが はなせます. Kansai casual uses the shorter 〜える/〜れる forms: はなせる, いける.
units.form: Godan: かく → かける. Ichidan: たべる → たべられる. する → できる. くる → こられる.
units.pitfall: Potential verbs usually take が: かんじが かけます. The object marker を is increasingly heard but が is safer.

units.title: Wanting to do something
units.can: express your own wish and ask about someone else’s.
units.explain: Add たい to the verb stem: たべます → たべたい, いきます → いきたい. The negative is 〜たくない. For a third person’s wish, Japanese often adds 〜たがっています rather than 〜たいです, because たい describes your own inner state most naturally.
units.form: V-ます stem + たいです. Negative: たくないです.
units.pitfall: たい describes your own wish. For someone else, use 〜たがっている or ask 〜たいですか.

units.title: Because: から and ので
units.can: give a reason without making the sentence feel like a lecture.
units.explain: から states a reason directly and can sound assertive. ので is softer and often preferred in polite explanations. Put the reason first: あめですから、いきません. With ので, use the plain form before it: あめなので、いきません.
units.form: Clause + から (direct, casual). Clause + ので (softer, more polite).
units.pitfall: から can sound blunt in an apology. With a superior, ので is safer.

units.title: Counting things
units.can: count people, flat things, machines and small objects with the right counter.
units.pattern: ひとつ ・ ふたり ・ さんまい ・ だい
units.explain: Japanese uses counters. ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ work for many small objects. People use にん (ひとり, ふたり, さんにん). Flat things use まい (paper, shirts, plates). Machines and vehicles use だい. Ask いくつですか for things, なんにんですか for people.
units.form: Number + counter: ひとつ ふたつ (things), ひとり ふたり (people), まい (flat), だい (machines).
units.pitfall: The counter is not optional. ひとつ for things, ひとり for people, いっぴき for animals.

units.title: Have you ever…?

units.title: Looks like: 〜そう
units.can: describe how something appears before you commit to a fact.
units.pattern: い-adjective stem + そう ・ な-adjective + そう
units.explain: For い-adjectives, drop the final い: おいしい → おいしそう (looks delicious). For な-adjectives, add そう directly: しずかそう. This is appearance, not certainty. Do not use it with your own feelings: たのしそう is “looks fun”, たのしい is “is fun for me”.
units.form: い-adjective stem + そう (おいしそう). な-adjective + そう (しずかそう). いい → よさそう.
units.pitfall: そう is appearance, not fact. おいしそうです = looks delicious; おいしいです = is delicious.

units.title: I heard / it seems: 〜らしい and 〜みたい
units.can: pass on information and describe an impression.
units.explain: らしい sounds like information from elsewhere: あめが ふる らしい = apparently it will rain. みたい is “like” or “seems”, often based on your impression: がくせい みたい = looks like a student. In polite speech, 〜ようです is the safe version of みたい.
units.form: Plain clause + らしい (hearsay). Plain clause + みたい (impression, casual).
units.pitfall: らしい can also mean “typical of”: かれらしい = just like him. Context decides.

units.title: The explanation 〜んです
units.can: give context, ask for a reason, and sound less abrupt.
units.explain: 〜んです presents information as explanation or context. どうしたんですか = what happened? あめが ふっているんです = the thing is, it is raining. It softens questions and makes answers feel connected to the conversation. Kansai uses 〜んや / 〜ねん.
units.form: Plain clause + んです／のです. Question: どうして 〜んですか.
units.pitfall: んです adds explanation or emphasis. Overusing it can sound defensive.

units.title: When: 〜とき
units.can: say what you do or did at a particular time.
units.explain: 〜とき means “when”. The tense of the clause before とき sets the time: にほんに いく とき = when I go to Japan; にほんに いった とき = when I went to Japan. The main clause can be any tense. Kansai uses 〜とき or 〜ときに.

units.pitfall: The tense is relative: たべる とき = before eating; たべた とき = after eating.

units.can: connect five or six sentences into a short story about your week.
units.pattern: はじめに → そして → でも → だから → おわりに
units.explain: This level is a checkpoint, not a new grammar point. Take one event from your week and tell it in six sentences: when, where, who, what happened, how you felt, what you will do next. Use て-form to link actions, から for reasons, が/けど for contrast, and 〜ました for the past.

units.pitfall: Do not translate “and then” word for word. Japanese stories often drop the subject after the first sentence.

units.title: The passive: it was done to me
units.can: describe an action from the receiving side, including annoyance.
units.explain: The passive changes the viewpoint: たべる → たべられる (be eaten). It also expresses damage or inconvenience: あめに ふられました = I got rained on. Form it from the ない-stem: かく → かかれる, よむ → よまれる. Kansai casual often prefers an active sentence, or 〜しやがった for the same feeling.
units.form: Godan: かく → かかれる. Ichidan: たべる → たべられる. する → される. くる → こられる.
units.pitfall: The passive can express annoyance: あめに ふられました = I got rained on. Do not always translate it as “was done”.

units.title: The causative: make or let someone do
units.can: say that someone makes or allows another person to do something.
units.explain: The causative means “make/let someone do”. たべる → たべさせる, いく → いかせる, する → させる. Context decides “make” or “let”: こどもに やさいを たべさせます = I make/let my child eat vegetables. Kansai casual: 〜させる / 〜さす.
units.form: Godan: かく → かかせる. Ichidan: たべる → たべさせる. する → させる. くる → こさせる.
units.pitfall: Make versus let is context, not form. たべさせる can mean “make eat” or “let eat”.

units.title: Purpose: ために and ように
units.can: explain why you do something and what you are aiming for.
units.explain: ために follows a noun + の or a verb expressing an intentional action: にほんに いく ために、おかねを ためています. ように follows a potential or non-volitional verb: みえる ように、まえに すわります. Rule of thumb: if you choose the action, ために; if you are arranging conditions, ように.
units.form: Noun + の ために. V-る + ために. V-る + ように.
units.pitfall: ために with a verb implies the same subject. ように is used when the result is not fully controlled.

units.title: Negotiate politely
units.can: ask a favour, refuse gently, and keep the relationship intact.
units.pattern: 〜ていただけませんか ・ 〜にくいです ・ 〜かもしれません
units.explain: N3 politeness is about leaving room. 〜ていただけませんか is a high-polite request. ちょっと むずかしいです is a soft refusal. 〜かもしれません adds uncertainty. Combine them: すみません、ちょっと むずかしいかもしれません。 This level is a rehearsal for workplace Japanese.
units.form: V-ていただけませんか (could you). V-にくいです (hard to). かもしれません (might).
units.pitfall: ていただけませんか is very polite. With friends, 〜てくれる？ is the natural register.

units.title: That explains it: 〜わけだ
units.can: draw a conclusion from evidence, and deny a false conclusion.
units.explain: わけだ means “so that is why” or “it follows that”. 〜わけではない means “it does not necessarily mean that”. It is a reasoning word, not a fact word: it shows you are connecting the dots. In Kansai, 〜わけや / 〜わけちゃう.
units.form: Plain clause + わけだ (that explains it). わけではない (it is not that).
units.pitfall: わけだ is a conclusion from evidence, not a casual “because”. Do not use it in place of から.

units.title: Should be: 〜はずだ
units.can: say what you expect to be true, and what cannot be true.
units.explain: はずだ expresses expectation based on reason: でんしゃは すぐ くる はずです = the train should come soon. はずがない is stronger: “it cannot be”. Use it when the facts do not fit. Kansai: 〜はずや / 〜はずない.
units.form: Plain clause + はずだ (should be). はずがない (cannot be).
units.pitfall: はずだ is expectation based on logic, not obligation. For “must do”, use なければならない.

units.title: Certainty and possibility
units.can: rank how sure you are, from “might” to “must be”.
units.pattern: 〜かもしれない ・ 〜に違いない ・ 〜だろう
units.explain: かもしれない = might. だろう = probably. に違いない = must be, with confidence. Japanese prefers hedging in polite settings; a bare に違いない can sound theatrical. Combine with たぶん for a natural “probably”.
units.form: かもしれない (might) < だろう (probably) < に違いない (must be).
units.pitfall: だろう is casual; in polite speech use でしょう. に違いない is strong and literary.

units.title: Workplace Japanese: the polite layer
units.can: use the three basic keigo moves: 尊敬語, 謙譲語 and 丁寧語.
units.pattern: いらっしゃいます ・ うかがいます ・ ございます
units.explain: Keigo has three gears. 尊敬語 raises the other person (いらっしゃる, おっしゃる). 謙譲語 lowers you (うかがう, もうす). 丁寧語 is the です/ます layer. You do not need perfect keigo to be polite; you need the common set and a calm tone. Kansai workplaces mix keigo with local warmth.
units.form: 尊敬語 raises the other person: いらっしゃる, おっしゃる. 謙譲語 lowers you: うかがう, もうす. 丁寧語: です／ます／ございます.
units.pitfall: Do not use 謙譲語 about the other person. せんせいが うかがいます is wrong; use いらっしゃいます.

units.title: Unbecoming: 〜まじき
units.can: condemn behaviour that violates a role or standard.
units.explain: まじき means “unbecoming of” or “should not be done by”. It attaches to verbs: いう → いうまじき, する → するまじき. It is formal and moralising: せんせいにあるまじき こうい = behaviour unbecoming of a teacher. Use it in writing and serious speech, not light chat.
units.form: Noun + まじき + noun (unbecoming).
units.pitfall: まじき is fixed and formal: あるまじき 行為. Do not conjugate it like a normal adjective.

units.title: The long conversation
units.can: hold your ground in a nuanced discussion, summarise both sides, and choose your next question.
units.pattern: 要約する → 比較する → 譲歩する → 質問する
units.explain: The last level is not a new pattern. It is the whole toolkit under pressure: summarise what you heard, compare two views, concede a fair point, and ask a question that moves the conversation forward. Use keigo for distance, plain form for intimacy, and Kansai-ben only when the relationship invites it. Fluency is the ability to keep listening while you speak.
units.form: 要約 → 比較 → 譲歩 → 質問.
units.pitfall: Do not rush to your opinion. Summarise the other side first; たしかに〜が、〜 is the hinge.
